options: A special SCD type reserved only for date dimensions
A dimension that alternates between SCD Type 1 and Type 2 randomly on each ETL run
A single dimension table that applies different SCD types to different columns, based on each attribute's own history requirement
A dimension table that has no SCD tracking of any kind
questions.explain: Hybrid SCD means classifying each attribute on a dimension individually — some columns might be Type 1, others Type 2, on the very same table.

questions.q: What question does this lesson say should decide which SCD type applies to a given attribute?
options: How many rows does the dimension table currently have?
Does any report need this value exactly as it was at the time a related fact occurred?
Was the attribute added to the table before or after the fact table was built?
Is the attribute stored as a string or a number?
questions.explain: That question separates attributes that need historical preservation (Type 2) from ones that are safe to overwrite (Type 1) or that never change at all (Type 0).

questions.q: In the worked Customer dimension example, why is CustomerSegment classified as Type 2 while EmailAddress is classified as Type 1?
options: CustomerSegment is a numeric column and EmailAddress is a text column
Type 2 is required for any column that starts with the word "Customer"
Reports need historical rollups (like revenue by segment) to reflect the segment at the time of each order, while an email correction has no analytical need to preserve the old value
There is no real reason — the classification is arbitrary
questions.explain: The deciding factor is whether historical analysis depends on the value as it was at the time, not the column's data type or name.

questions.q: According to Microsoft's own guidance quoted in this lesson, is it normal for a dimension to support more than one SCD type at once?
options: Yes — Microsoft's guidance directly states a dimension could support both Type 1 and Type 2 changes
Yes, but only for date dimensions
Microsoft's guidance never addresses this question
No — Microsoft's guidance says every dimension must use exactly one SCD type for all columns
questions.explain: Microsoft's dimensional modeling documentation explicitly acknowledges that a dimension can support both Type 1 and Type 2 changes on different attributes.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that treating an entire dimension as pure Type 2 is not actually simpler in practice?
options: Every trivial correction, like a typo fix, would spawn a new versioned row, ballooning the dimension with versions that carry no real analytical meaning
Pure Type 2 dimensions cannot have a surrogate key
Pure Type 2 dimensions are not supported by SQL Server
Pure Type 2 requires deleting the fact table first
questions.explain: Applying Type 2 to every column, even ones that only need corrections, creates unnecessary versions and dimension bloat — the hybrid approach avoids that by reserving Type 2 for attributes that truly need it.
